designs.title: Store orders and inventory
designs.question: Where should an online store keep its orders, carts and stock counts?
designs.short_answer: Orders, order lines, payments references and stock live in one relational database, PostgreSQL or MySQL. Carts can live in Redis. Product search goes to a search engine, and reporting goes to a column store.
workload: Bursty. Quiet most of the day, then 10 to 50 times normal during a sale.
Mostly by key: an order, a customer's orders, a product's stock.
Around 10 to 1 on the order tables, much higher on the catalog.
Strict for stock and orders. Two customers must not buy the last item.
Checkout under a few hundred milliseconds end to end.
Steady. Orders are rarely deleted, so the tables only grow.
placement: Transactions across several tables, foreign keys, and a check that stock never goes below zero. This is what a relational database is built for.
Redis or Valkey, or the same database
A cart is read and rewritten on every click and can be rebuilt if lost. Keeping it out of the order tables keeps them small and hot.
Full-text search with filters. The database stays the source of truth; the index is a copy.
A column store, fed by change data capture
Reports scan millions of order lines. Running them on the primary competes with checkout.
breaks: The hot SKU during a sale
Lock waits on one stock row, connection pool exhausted
Keep the stock transaction short, and reserve stock before payment, with a timeout to release it. See the lock pile-up lab .
Reports on the primary
CPU spikes at the top of the hour, checkout latency follows
Move reports to a replica or a column store.
OFFSET paging in the admin order list
Page 1 is fast, page 500 times out
Page by key. See paging .
where_to_run: Managed relational with a standby in another zone
Cloud-native managed (Aurora, AlloyDB) for read replicas, or self-managed on VMs if the steady bill justifies a team
designs.keywords: shop store ecommerce e-commerce orders cart checkout inventory stock sku oversell flash sale

designs.title: Payments and ledgers
designs.question: Where should money movements live, and how do I make sure no cent appears or disappears?
designs.short_answer: A relational database with a double-entry ledger that is append-only, with idempotency keys and synchronous replication. Correctness first, speed second.
workload: Steady. Every movement is a write, never an update in place.
Close to 1 to 1 on the ledger.
Strict. A committed movement must survive any single failure, and the books must always balance.
Tens to hundreds of milliseconds is fine. Correctness matters more.
Forever. Ledgers are kept for years, often by law.
placement: PostgreSQL or MySQL, with synchronous replication
Transactions, constraints, and a commit that waits for a standby, so a failover cannot lose an acknowledged payment. See what a commit waits for .
The same database, in the same transaction
A retried request must find the key that the first attempt wrote, or the money moves twice.
A replica or a column store
Long scans that must not slow down new payments.
Object storage, plus a table that points to them
Large, rarely read, kept for audit.
breaks: A retry without an idempotency key
Duplicate charges in reconciliation
Make the key mandatory in the API, and unique in the database.
Async replication and a failover
Payments acknowledged, then missing on the new primary
Use synchronous replication for this database, and accept the latency.
A hot account, such as the platform fee account
Lock waits on one balance row
Spread it over several sub-accounts and sum them, or derive the balance from entries.
where_to_run: Managed relational with synchronous standby (RDS Multi-AZ or equivalent)
The same, plus cross-region copies. Self-managed only with a team that rehearses failover
designs.keywords: payments ledger money balance wallet transfer accounting double entry fintech billing invoice refund

designs.title: Bookings and reservations
designs.question: How do I stop two people from booking the same seat, room or time slot?
designs.short_answer: A relational database with the rule enforced by the database itself: a unique constraint on (resource, slot), or an exclusion constraint on time ranges in PostgreSQL. Short holds with an expiry for the checkout window.
workload: Spiky. A ticket sale opens and everyone tries at once.
Availability searches, much more often than bookings.
High, and very high during an on-sale.
Strict on the booking itself. Availability displays can be a few seconds stale.
Booking under a second, even under a spike.
placement: The database rejects a double booking, whatever the application code does.
A cache or a read replica
Many readers, slightly stale is fine, final check happens at booking.
A queue in front of the booking service
Turns a spike into a steady stream the database can take.
breaks: Check-then-insert in application code
Double bookings under load
Use the constraint. A SELECT then INSERT is exactly the write skew pattern.
Locks held during payment
Pool exhausted during an on-sale
Use a hold row with an expiry instead of an open transaction.
Availability computed from scratch on each search
CPU spikes on the primary during an on-sale
Cache availability and recheck at booking.
where_to_run: Managed relational, plus a managed queue for on-sales
The same. The spike is handled by the queue, not by a bigger database
designs.keywords: booking reservation seats tickets hotel appointment calendar slots double booking on-sale availability

designs.title: Accounts and sessions
designs.question: Where should user accounts live, and where should sessions and tokens go?
designs.short_answer: Accounts in the main relational database. Sessions in Redis or Valkey with an expiry, or no server-side session at all if you use short-lived signed tokens.
workload: Low for accounts. High for sessions: every login, and often every request touches a session.
Every authenticated request reads a session or validates a token.
Strict for accounts (a unique email). Loose for sessions: losing one means one more login.
Session lookups must take about a millisecond, since every request pays it.
Accounts grow slowly. Sessions churn and expire.
placement: A unique constraint on email, and transactions for sign-up and role changes.
Redis or Valkey with a TTL on each key
Lookups by key in memory, and expiry is built in. Losing them costs a login, not data.
A counter per user or per IP that expires on its own.
An append-only table or log, partitioned by time
Kept for security reviews, rarely read.
breaks: Sessions in the main database
A delete job for expired sessions causes bloat and I/O spikes
Move sessions to a store with built-in expiry.
Redis without a memory limit
Redis runs out of memory, or swaps
Set maxmemory and an eviction policy that removes keys with a TTL first (volatile-lru).
Case-sensitive email lookups
Duplicate accounts for one person
Unique index on lower(email).
where_to_run: Managed relational, plus managed Redis or Valkey
designs.keywords: users accounts login auth authentication sessions tokens identity passwords sso

designs.title: Multi-tenant SaaS
designs.question: One database for all customers, one schema each, or one database each?
designs.short_answer: Start with a shared schema and a tenant_id on every row, enforced by row-level security in PostgreSQL or by a mandatory filter in the data layer. Move very large tenants to their own database when they need it.
workload: Varies by tenant. A few tenants usually produce most of the load.
Strict inside a tenant. Tenants never see each other's data.
By number of tenants, plus a few that grow very large.
placement: One schema to migrate, one pool of connections, cheap to add a tenant.
Isolation of load and data, at the cost of more databases to operate.
Says which database each tenant lives in.
breaks: A missing tenant filter
Data leak between customers
Row-level security, or a data layer that cannot build a query without tenant_id.
One tenant's heavy job
Every other tenant slows down
Rate-limit per tenant and move heavy tenants out.
Schema per tenant at thousands of tenants
Migrations take hours, catalog bloat
Prefer shared schema with tenant_id.
where_to_run: Managed for the shared tier. Kubernetes with an operator, or many managed instances, for tenants that get their own database
designs.keywords: saas multi-tenant tenants customers b2b organizations workspace isolation noisy neighbour

designs.title: Product catalog
designs.question: Where should a catalog go when every product type has different attributes?
designs.short_answer: PostgreSQL with common columns plus a JSONB column for the varied attributes, or MongoDB with one document per product. A search engine on top for browsing and filtering.
workload: Low. Merchants edit products a few times a day.
Very high. Every page view, every search, every filter.
Loose. A price change can take a second to appear in search.
Product pages from cache in milliseconds. Search under 200 ms.
Moderate. Thousands to millions of products.
placement: Shared fields (price, title, stock link) as columns or fields. Type-specific fields in JSONB or the document.
Counting matches per color, size and brand across millions of products is what an inverted index is for.
Pages change rarely and are read constantly.
breaks: LIKE %term% on titles
Sequential scans in the slow log
Move text search to a search engine, or use full-text search in PostgreSQL for small catalogs.
The search index out of sync
A product shows a price it no longer has
Write changes to an outbox table in the same transaction, and have one process ship them to the index.
Every attribute in JSONB
Joins and sorts on JSON fields are slow and hard to index
Promote frequently used attributes to columns.
where_to_run: Managed relational, plus a managed search service
The same, with a CDN in front
designs.keywords: catalog products attributes facets filters prices variants pim

designs.title: Social feed
designs.question: How do I build a home timeline that shows posts from everyone I follow?
designs.short_answer: Posts and the follow graph in a relational database. Timelines precomputed per user in Redis or a wide-column store (fan-out on write), except for accounts with huge followings, whose posts are merged in at read time.
workload: Posts are moderate. Fan-out multiplies each post by the number of followers.
Very high. Opening the app reads a timeline.
Loose. A post can appear a few seconds late.
The first screen of the timeline in well under a second.
Fast, driven by user count times follows.
placement: The record of who posted what and who follows whom.
Redis lists or sorted sets, or Cassandra and ScyllaDB at large scale
A timeline is a list of post IDs per user, read as one key. Writes are many and small, which suits memory or an LSM store.
The database for text, object storage and a CDN for media
Media is large and read often, which is a CDN job.
breaks: A celebrity posts
The fan-out queue backs up for minutes
Do not fan out for accounts above a follower threshold. Merge at read time.
Pull queries at scale
A big IN list of followees sorted by time
Precompute.
Timelines that never expire
Memory grows with inactive users
Cap each timeline, and drop timelines of users who have not opened the app in weeks.
where_to_run: Managed or self-managed wide-column store on VMs with local NVMe and replicas
designs.keywords: feed timeline followers posts social fan-out likes news feed

designs.title: Search and AI retrieval
designs.question: Where should full-text search and vector search for AI features go?
designs.short_answer: Start in PostgreSQL: full-text search and pgvector, next to the data. Move to a dedicated search engine or vector database when the size, the query rate, or the ranking needs outgrow it.
workload: Documents added and updated, each needing an embedding.
Queries by text and by similarity, often combined with filters.
Loose. A new document can take seconds to become searchable.
Under a few hundred milliseconds, including the embedding of the query.
Moderate to large. Embeddings are big: hundreds to thousands of numbers per item.
placement: No second system, and filters and permissions are just SQL.
Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, or a vector database
Distributed indexes, hybrid text and vector ranking, more tuning knobs.
breaks: HNSW index larger than memory
Latency jumps as the index pages come from disk
Size memory to the index, or reduce dimensions, or quantize.
Embeddings from mixed model versions
Results that quietly get worse
Record the model per row and re-embed in one pass.
Permission filters applied after search
Users see snippets of documents they cannot open
Filter inside the query.
where_to_run: A managed search or vector service once the index outgrows memory
designs.keywords: search full-text rag retrieval embeddings vector semantic pgvector documents chunks similarity

designs.title: Chat and messaging
designs.question: Where should chat messages go, when there are billions of them and every conversation is read newest first?
designs.short_answer: At small and medium scale, PostgreSQL with messages partitioned by time and indexed by (conversation_id, sent_at). At large scale, a wide-column store such as Cassandra or ScyllaDB, partitioned by conversation and bucketed by time.
workload: High and steady. Every message is an insert.
The latest page of one conversation, very often.
Per conversation, in order. Across conversations, loose.
Delivery feels instant: tens of milliseconds to store.
Fast and forever, unless you set retention.
placement: PostgreSQL with time partitions, then Cassandra or ScyllaDB
One conversation, newest first, is a range read on one partition. LSM stores take heavy insert rates well.
Changes every few seconds and does not need to survive a restart.
breaks: One huge group chat
A hot partition and slow reads
Bucket by time inside the conversation.
Deleting old messages with DELETE
Bloat and long-running deletes
Drop whole partitions, or use TTLs in the wide-column store.
Unread counts computed on every read
COUNT(*) over a conversation on every app open
Keep a per-member last-read marker and a counter.
where_to_run: Managed Cassandra-compatible service, or self-managed Cassandra or ScyllaDB on VMs
designs.keywords: chat messages messaging conversations channels inbox websocket presence

designs.title: IoT and telemetry
designs.question: Where should millions of sensor readings per minute go?
designs.short_answer: A time-series database (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB) or a column store (ClickHouse), with time partitioning, compression, downsampling and retention. Device metadata stays relational.
workload: Very high, steady, in time order. Mostly appends.
Ranges of time for one device or a group, and aggregates per minute or hour.
Low. Most data is written and rarely read.
Loose. A late reading is fine.
Dashboards in a second or two.
Huge. Retention is the main design decision.
placement: Time partitions, compression of similar values, and dropping old partitions whole.
Redis, or a small table updated in place
"What is the temperature now" should not scan the history.
Cheap, and readable later by analytics tools.
breaks: Row-by-row inserts
Commit rate caps throughput long before disks do
Batch. See what one commit costs in Notebook 2 .
High cardinality labels
Index size explodes in metric stores
Do not use user IDs or request IDs as tags.
No retention
Storage bill grows every month without end
Decide retention per resolution on day one.
where_to_run: A managed time-series or ClickHouse service
Self-managed on VMs when volume is high and steady, and storage cost dominates
designs.keywords: iot telemetry sensors devices metrics time series readings timeseries monitoring

designs.title: Audit and event logs
designs.question: Where should an append-only history of everything that happened go?
designs.short_answer: An append-only table partitioned by time in the relational database, or a stream (Kafka) with a long retention plus a copy in object storage. Never updated, rarely read, kept for years.
workload: Rare: investigations, compliance exports, a user's activity page.
The entry must be committed with the action it records.
Writes must be cheap. Reads can be slow.
placement: A partitioned table in the same database as the action
Written in the same transaction, so an action never happens without its record.
Object storage in Parquet, or a column store
Cheap, and still queryable by analytics tools.
Other systems consume the events without querying your database.
breaks: Audit written after the transaction commits
Actions with no record when the process crashes in between
Write it in the same transaction, or use the outbox pattern.
One giant unpartitioned table
Backups and vacuum take hours
Partition by time.
Personal data in the log
A deletion request you cannot honor
Store references, not personal data, or plan how to redact.
where_to_run: In the same managed database as the action
Old partitions exported to object storage
designs.keywords: audit log events history compliance append-only trail gdpr who changed

designs.title: Leaderboards and counters
designs.question: Where should fast-changing counts go: views, likes, scores, rate limits?
designs.short_answer: Redis or Valkey: sorted sets for leaderboards, INCR with a TTL for counters and rate limits. Flush totals to the database in batches if they must be kept.
workload: Very high, on a few hot keys.
Top N, my rank, the current count.
Approximate is usually fine. A like count can be a second behind.
Small. One entry per player or per object.
placement: Rank queries are built in, and each update is O(log n) in memory.
Atomic increments with no lock, and expiry built in.
One write per minute per object instead of one per event.
breaks: UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 on one hot row
Lock waits, lock pile-up
Move the counter to Redis, or spread it across several rows and sum them.
KEYS * in production
Redis stalls for everyone
Use SCAN.
Counters with no TTL
Memory grows forever
Expire window keys.
where_to_run: The same. MemoryDB-style durable options if the totals must survive a failover
designs.keywords: leaderboard counters scores ranking likes views rate limit top n

designs.title: Analytics and reporting
designs.question: Where should reports and dashboards run, so they do not slow down the application?
designs.short_answer: Not on the production primary. Copy data to a column store (ClickHouse, BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake, DuckDB for small cases) through change data capture or batch loads, and run reports there.
workload: Batch loads or a stream of changes from production.
Big scans with aggregates over a few columns.
Reads are few but each one reads a lot.
Minutes behind production is usually fine.
Seconds for a dashboard, minutes for a heavy report.
Large. All history, often from several systems.
placement: Reads only the columns a query names, compressed, in parallel.
The copy must never be able to slow the source down.
Change data capture (Debezium, or the managed equivalent) or scheduled batch exports
Ships changes without running scans on the primary.
breaks: Reports on the primary
The application slows down at report time
Move them. This is the most common cause of mystery slowdowns on a schedule.
Single-row inserts into a column store
Too many small parts, merges fall behind
Batch the inserts.
Replica used for both failover and heavy reports
A long query delays replay, and the failover target is behind
Separate the two roles.
where_to_run: A managed warehouse or ClickHouse Cloud, fed by CDC
The same. Self-managed ClickHouse on VMs if scan costs are high and the team exists
designs.keywords: analytics reporting dashboards bi warehouse olap aggregates reports metrics

designs.title: Agent memory and state
designs.question: Where should an AI agent keep its conversations, its progress and what it remembers?
designs.short_answer: One PostgreSQL with pgvector holds the run log, the checkpoints and the long-term memories, with tenant_id in every key. Redis holds the working memory of runs in progress. Turn on iterative scan for filtered memory search, and give every memory an expiry.
workload: Many small writes per run: each step adds messages, a tool call and a checkpoint.
Each step reads the recent conversation, the latest checkpoint, and searches long-term memory.
Close to one to one for run state. Memories are read more than written.
Strict for checkpoints: resume from exactly the last step. Loose for memory search: a memory saved a second ago can be missed.
Memory search well under 50 ms, because it runs before every model call, and the model call itself takes seconds.
Fast. Every run leaves a log, and memories grow per user for as long as nobody forgets them.
placement: Runs, messages and tool calls (the run log)
Every step of every run, in order. You need it to debug a bad answer, to bill, and to audit what the agent did. Append-only and large, so it is partitioned from day one.
After a crash or a deploy, the run resumes from its last step instead of starting again. Small, written every step, read back by primary key.
pgvector in the same PostgreSQL, filtered by tenant
Facts and summaries the agent should recall later. In the same database, a memory, its tenant and its permissions are one row and one query.
Working memory of an active run
Redis or Valkey, with an expiry
Scratch state, rate limits and locks for runs in progress. Fast, short-lived, and safe to lose because the checkpoint has the durable state.
Kept for audit and evaluation, rarely read, far cheaper than database storage.
breaks: Filtered memory search returns too few rows
The agent "forgets" things it was told yesterday
Turn on hnsw.iterative_scan (pgvector 0.8 and later), or for small tenants search exactly within the tenant. In Notebook 8 the plain filtered search returned 1.3 rows out of 10.
Parallel runs open hundreds of connections
Connection errors and memory pressure on the database when traffic peaks
A pooler (PgBouncer) in front, and a cap on concurrent runs per tenant.
The run log dominates storage and backups
Backups and restores get slow, and the bill grows every month
Monthly partitions, export old months to object storage, drop the partition.
Memories are never forgotten
Old, wrong facts outrank new ones; the store grows forever
An expiry and a last-used time on every memory, recency in the ranking, and merging duplicates when a memory is saved.
Embeddings from two models in one index
Search quality drops quietly
Store the model name on every row and re-embed in one pass when you change models.
A memory saved or found under the wrong tenant
One customer's data in another customer's answer
tenant_id in every key and every query, and row-level security as a backstop.
where_to_run: Managed PostgreSQL with pgvector, plus managed Redis or Valkey
The same, with a pooler in front. A dedicated vector service only once the memory index outgrows one machine's memory
designs.keywords: agent agents ai llm memory long-term memory conversation history checkpoints state tool calls langgraph assistant copilot
